name: Sam Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, it's been a blur. Anatomy dissection sessions on Monday and Wednesday, which were a shock for the first week, then biochemistry lectures, and a small-group clinical skills session on Friday where we practise talking to actors who pretend to be patients. I live in a hall with a lot of other medical students, and half of us have a group chat where we share summaries. I built a small tool that turns my lecture recordings into practice questions, and I use AI for pretty much everything study-related.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful, just not world-changing, and people should keep learning the basics. I'd share my study tool with the group chat and tell them to take it or leave it. I wouldn't post it, because I'm not trying to build a following.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine. Medicine depends on people and trust, and a plateau means the plan works as expected. I'd keep tinkering because I enjoy it, and it'd be a good hobby alongside a steady career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my degree and keep improving the tool a little each month, maybe adding flashcards from textbooks. I'd shadow a doctor over the summer, because my mum's friend is a GP and said I could. I'd keep exercising, which I'm bad at when it's busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. My family pays for everything, I have good results, and medicine is a safe path in most scenarios. I try not to take that for granted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a plateau make your study tool less interesting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The length and cost of medical training in general, and whether I'm one of those people who burn out. The exams are hard, and the hours on placement are long. A plateau doesn't change any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still keep you busy worrying in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes, because I like it when things move. But I'd rather have a steady world to be a doctor in than a thrilling one where I'm not sure what a doctor is. Boring is a good deal.

say: I'd say it's **useful, not world-changing**, and people should learn the basics.
I'd share my study tool with the group chat but **not post it**.
think: Privately I'm **fine**: medicine depends on people and trust.
I'd keep tinkering as a **hobby** beside a steady career.
do: Keep improving my study tool each month, maybe adding **textbook flashcards**.
Shadow a **GP** over the summer, through my mum's friend.
feel: **Calm**, aware that my family backing makes it easy.
S0.quote: I'd rather have a steady world to be a doctor in than a thrilling one where I'm not sure what a doctor is.
fieldNote: He values **stability** over excitement despite being a tinkerer.
He names **burnout** as his real worry, independent of AI.
He is **modest** about sharing his tool and doesn't seek a following.

steps.text: Add textbook flashcards to my study tool
Shadow a GP over the summer
Keep up the Friday clinical skills sessions and the gym

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should lean in and learn how to use the tools well, and also ask who is liable when they're wrong. I'd tell my group chat to share what works and what fails. I'd bring it up in our ethics seminar, since they love that topic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm quite optimistic. Doctors do a lot of reading, writing and searching, and software can help with all of it. I'd become the doctor who can check what it says, which I think is a stable thing to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building and testing, and look for a society or a project that works on health data. I'd ask my lecturers how the course will change, and which specialities look more or less affected. I'd also talk to a junior doctor about how their work is already shifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, with a streak of caution. It's a good time to be someone who isn't afraid of the tools, but I'd keep checking my own judgement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Which parts of a doctor's work do you think it takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Notes, summaries, spotting patterns in scans and blood tests, and first drafts of letters. The talking to scared people and the final decision stay with the doctor, I think. I'd say about a third of a junior doctor's day is typing right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about your own tool change in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My tool becomes a small version of what hospitals use, so it's a nice practice run. I'd show it to a lecturer and ask what a safe version would need. I'd rather learn the limits of these tools early, because a doctor who can check what software says is the person patients will still want.

say: I'd say **lean in** and learn the tools, but ask who's liable.
I'd tell my group chat to share what works and **what fails**.
think: Privately I'm **optimistic**: doctors read, write and search, which software helps with.
I'd become the doctor who can **check the output**, a stable role.
do: Look for a society or project on **health data**.
Ask a **junior doctor** how their work is already shifting.
feel: **Calm and excited**, with a streak of caution.
S1.quote: I'd rather learn the limits of these tools early, because a doctor who can check what software says is the person patients will still want.
fieldNote: He turns **AI use** into medical practice, a natural link.
He names **liability** early, which comes back later.
His calm here rests on **the checking role** doctors keep.

steps.text: Join a society or project working on health data

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need clear rules about who is responsible when systems make medical decisions, and that medical schools should tell us what's going on. I'd post a few calm questions on the course forum. I'd ask lecturers directly, which I'd normally be shy about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be anxious. The training is six years and I'd be in year two when everything shifts, so I'd graduate into a world I can't picture. I'd think the doctor's role might become mostly about talking to patients and taking responsibility, and that sounds fine, but there'd be fewer jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in medicine, because it's still one of the safer paths with trust and law protecting it. I'd learn as much as I can about clinical AI, ask for a placement where it's used, and talk to my parents about money, in case plans change. I'd also keep my options open with a short course in data or health policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. It's the number of years that gets me. If I were doing a three-year course I'd feel different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years: where does your six-year degree stand then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, nobody knows what a doctor will do in 2031, so let's find out together. I'd start a shared document where we collect what we hear from placements and lecturers. At least we'd be less alone with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to the group chat that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the doctor is the one who's on the hook when it goes wrong. Whoever is on the hook when the software gets a diagnosis wrong is the person patients will actually need, and I want that to be a trained human. That's the bit I'd try to be good at.

say: I'd say we need **clear rules** about who is responsible for medical decisions.
I'd ask lecturers **directly**, which I'd normally be shy about.
think: Privately I'd be **anxious**: six years of training would span the change.
I think doctors would mostly **talk and take responsibility**, with fewer jobs.
do: Stay in medicine and ask for a placement where **clinical AI** is used.
Talk to my parents about **money** and take a short data or policy course.
feel: **Anxious but not frozen**, mostly because of the six years.
S2.quote: Whoever is on the hook when the software gets a diagnosis wrong is the person patients will actually need, and I want that to be a trained human.
fieldNote: His anxiety is about **training length**, not hands-on exposure.
He **organises a shared document** with friends, a collective instinct.
His strongest idea is **responsibility and liability**.

steps.text: Ask for a clinical placement where AI diagnosis tools are used
Take a short course in health data or health policy
Talk with my parents about money in case plans change
Start a shared document with friends collecting what we hear from lecturers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, but only if medical schools use it well. I'd tell my friends that we should ask for updated teaching each year, and I'd push my lecturers on it. I'd also tell them not to make panic decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel uneasy but quite hopeful. Five years takes me into my clinical years, so I'd learn medicine alongside the tools and know both. I'd be one of the first generation who trained with them from the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying, learn the tools properly, and spend some time on a research project about AI in diagnosis. I'd save part of my allowance, because the extra years of training are expensive even with family help. I'd also look at speciality options, with a bias to those that involve talking and procedures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can handle it. It feels like a challenge with a deadline, which suits me. I'd sleep fine and work hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two did not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A longer warning gives me a chance to be part of the answer, not just a victim of the question. I could do a small research project, maybe with my tool, and see how real hospitals handle it. That's more useful than worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change specialty because of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes, away from things like reading scans and towards procedures, emergency or general practice. I'd decide in my clinical years, but I'd keep the question in my head from now.

say: I'd say there's **time**, but only if medical schools use it well.
I'd tell friends **not to panic** over choices.
think: Privately I'm **uneasy but hopeful**: I'd learn medicine and the tools together.
I could be in the **first generation** trained with them.
do: Work on a **research project** about AI in diagnosis.
Save part of my **allowance**, since extra training years cost money.
feel: **Uneasy but capable**, like a challenge with a deadline.
S3.quote: A longer warning gives me a chance to be part of the answer, not just a victim of the question.
fieldNote: He frames time as **a chance to act**, not as a cushion.
He leans toward **procedural specialities** that robots would reach later.
He decides **later, in clinical years**, which fits a steady-adaptive style.

steps.text: Join a research project about AI in diagnosis
Save part of my monthly allowance
Look at procedure-based and emergency specialities and decide in clinical years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decade to get things right, so let's do it properly. I'd tell my friends to enjoy their degrees. I'd also push for medical schools to add a module on AI in practice, and I'd offer to help build it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm calm, even a little excited. By then I'd be 29 and a few years into being a doctor, and the tools would be mature enough for me to use them with confidence. I'd feel I had grown up with the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish medicine, train in a speciality that suits me, and keep tinkering with health tech in my spare time. I'd also build a modest savings pot, and maybe invest a little in an index fund once I earn. I'd look for a hospital or a company where doctors and engineers work together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A decade is long enough to adjust twice, so I'd worry more about passing my next exam than about 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. Do you get restless?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, because I like projects. But I'd turn it into building something, like improving the tool for other students. That would keep me happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it goes badly for doctors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hospital managers who chase savings and tech firms who sell half-tested products. I'd put the blame there, not on individual doctors who try to cope. It's a system problem, and systems need rules.

I'd offer to help build a **module on AI** in practice.
think: Privately I'm **calm**, even a little excited, because ten years lets me grow up alongside the tools.
I'd feel I had **grown up** with the change.
do: Finish medicine, pick a speciality, and keep tinkering with **health tech**.
Build a modest **savings pot** and consider an index fund once I earn.
feel: **Calm**, because a decade is long enough to adjust twice.

fieldNote: He turns **restlessness into building** projects for other students.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because medicine takes six years and I'd come out into a world nobody has described yet. What would help is a straight answer from medical schools about what they plan to teach, plus a way to change direction without losing years of tuition. And I'd like some rules about who is responsible when software gets a diagnosis wrong.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not a doomer and I'm not a hype guy either. I use these tools because they work, and I stop when they don't. I'd say most of my friends are in that boat: curious, practical, and a bit worried about the length of the training.

headlineQuote: I use these tools because they work, and I stop when they don't.
portrait: Sam is 19, in first-year **medicine**, with top results, a strong family cushion and a tinkerer's habits.
He is centrist and adaptive: he uses AI **every day** and built a small study tool.
He is **practical**, neither doomer nor hype, and worries mostly about the length of medical training.
His mood is calm in mild cases and anxious in the **two-year case**, because medicine takes six years.
His parents and his hall group chat are his support, and he acts by building, testing and asking.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries him most, because six years of training would run straight into it.
whatWouldHelp: A **straight answer** from medical schools about what they will teach.
Clear rules on **who is responsible** when software gets a diagnosis wrong.
